claims.text: The target alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a nanocrystalline grain size on the order of tens of nanometers.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
At 800–1000 °C, WTaTiVZr exhibits greater plastic strain to failure than commercially used pure tungsten.
At 800–1000 °C, WTaTiVZr absorbs more energy before fracture and is tougher than commercially used pure tungsten.
The enhanced plastic strain and toughness arise from the alloy's nanocrystalline microstructure and lattice distortion caused by multielement mixing.
High grain-boundary density in the nanocrystalline alloy enhances grain-boundary sliding.
Lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr enhances grain-boundary-mediated deformation and energy absorption.
Solid-solution hardening and the nanocrystalline microstructure shift WTaTiVZr deformation from dislocation-mediated plasticity to grain-boundary-mediated plasticity.
Pure tungsten commonly deforms through dislocation-mediated plasticity under the proposed conditions.
Grain-boundary-mediated deformation produces a more homogeneous plastic-strain distribution in WTaTiVZr.
Grain-boundary-mediated deformation promotes crack blunting in WTaTiVZr.
Pure tungsten has lower plastic strain, lower energy absorption, and more localized brittle failure than WTaTiVZr under identical high-temperature loading.
Post-test microscopy will show grain-boundary sliding or deformation in WTaTiVZr.
Post-test microscopy will show predominantly dislocation activity in pure tungsten.
A temperature range of 800–1000 °C is representative of sustained plasma-facing-component service.
The proposed mechanism applies only at strain rates for which grain-boundary processes are activated.
Oxidation or extensive grain growth can suppress or alter the proposed deformation mechanism.
A different equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy, CuMoTaWV, has been reported as a nanocrystalline BCC film with an average grain size of 18 nm.
Very long thermal exposure or high neutron flux may alter the WTaTiVZr microstructure and its mechanical response.
